newsitem.title: USA: Mercury Finance violates loan covenants, suspends dividend.
newsitem.headline: Mercury Finance violates loan covenants, suspends dividend.

text.p: Mercury Finance Co., the troubled used car financing firm, said Thursday that it was in violation of its loan covenants a day after it failed to meet $61 million in debt obligations.

The company, which has been in turmoil since it announced last week that accounting irregularities had caused it to overstate its earnings by millions of dollars, also said it was suspending a stock dividend payment due next month.

"The company has been unable to refinance an aggregate of $61 million in matured commercial paper through Feb. 5. An additional $127 million comes due between now and Feb. 14," Mercury said in a statement.
"As a result of previously disclosed events, the company is in violation of its loan covenants."

The company announced last Wednesday that it had found problems in its bookkeeping that caused it to overstate earnings by $90 million over four years. Earnings for last year, it said, were only $56.7 million -- rather than the $120.7 million it had originally reported.
The announcement caused Mercury's stock to plunge by about 86 percent, which prompted President and Chief Executive John Brincat to give up those posts.

The revelation of questionable accounting at the company -- which Mercury blamed on its former controller -- also prompted the Federal Bureau of Investigation Monday to send agents to the firm's headquarters in Lake Forest, Ill., a Chicago suburb.
Mercury said then that it was cooperating fully with the FBI investigators in supplying documents requested under a search warrant.
Mercury's former controller, James Doyle, whom the company said it dismissed, has denied through his lawyer that he was responsible for the accounting problems at the firm.
Doyle's lawyer accused Mercury of a "charade" regarding the faulty books and said his client was cooperating with federal authorities.
The company also said Thursday that it was seeking other sources of short-term financing.

"We are currently in serious discussion with lenders with regard to a short-term financing package," William A. Brandt Jr., a corporate rescue specialist who took over as president and chief executive, said in a statement.
"It is expected that the funds from the short-term financing will be used exclusively for operating purposes and will not be available for paying principal or interest on company debt."
Mercury, which engaged Salomon Brothers last week to advise it on financial matters, also said it continued to seek a long-term financing package.
It added that it was reviewing "all capital-raising alternatives" as it tries to repair its balance sheet.
"The company is pursuing a financial strategy that is aimed at enabling operations to continue and returning its financial status to a normal footing as quickly as possible," it said in a statement.
Mercury, which makes used car loans to individuals of often relatively low creditworthiness, also said Thursday that operations were continuing at all of the company's 280 locations nationwide.

The company was sued Wednesday by shareholders who accused it and its auditors, KPMG Peat Marwick LLP, of alleged breach of fiduciary duty for failure to disclose material information about the company's finances.
Other class action lawsuits by Mercury shareholders were filed Friday and earlier this week in federal courts in Illinois.

Mercury Finance's stock gained 12.5 cents to $2.625 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most actively traded issue in early trading. It had been trading in the $14 range before the announcement of the accounting problems.
